\section{Declarations}

\begin{lemma}[Initial true run in a paired encoding]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.takeWhile_pairEncode_replicate}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.takeWhile_pairEncode_replicate}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.dbl_replicate, Turing.pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode_eq_dbl}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and Boolean list $w$, the initial segment of true entries
in the pairing of the length-$n$ all-true list with $w$ is exactly the length-$2n$
all-true list.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Unary input with one register]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.vword_unary₁}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Mode.seg0, Complexity.LogProg.argSegs, Complexity.LogProg.callSegs, Complexity.LogProg.dbl_replicate, Complexity.LogProg.render, Complexity.LogProg.takeWhile_pairEncode_replicate, Complexity.LogProg.vword, Turing.pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode_eq_dbl}
\difficulty{3}
For any natural number $n$, bit string $w$, decider index $j$, register index $r$,
states $l_1,l_0$, and assignment $V$ of a bit string to each register, the virtual word
formed using the unary-prefix mode on the encoded pair $(1^n,w)$ and the single register
$r$ is the encoded pair $(1^n,V(r))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Unary input with two registers]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.vword_unary₂}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LogProg.Mode.seg0, Complexity.LogProg.argSegs, Complexity.LogProg.callSegs, Complexity.LogProg.dbl_replicate, Complexity.LogProg.render, Complexity.LogProg.takeWhile_pairEncode_replicate, Complexity.LogProg.vword, Turing.pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode_eq_dbl}
\difficulty{3}
For any natural number $n$, bit string $w$, decider index $j$, register indices $r,s$,
states $l_1,l_0$, and assignment $V$ of a bit string to each register, the virtual word
formed using the unary-prefix mode on the encoded pair $(1^n,w)$ and the two registers
$r,s$ is the encoded pair $(1^n,	ext{the encoded pair }(V(r),V(s)))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Indicator and membership decision]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.indicator_eq_decide}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.indicator_eq_decide}
\leanok
\uses{Turing.MultiTapeTM.indicator}
\difficulty{4}
For any set $S$ and element $a$, the Boolean indicator of $S$ at $a$ equals the Boolean
decision for the proposition $a\in S$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomially bounded register computations]
\lean{Complexity.LogProg.arm_decides_poly}
\label{Complexity.LogProg.arm_decides_poly}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.LOGSPACE, Complexity.LogProg.AHalt, Complexity.LogProg.AHalt.mono, Complexity.LogProg.ARM, Complexity.LogProg.PreS, Complexity.LogProg.arm_decides, Complexity.LogProg.length_bits_le_log, Complexity.LogProg.log_poly_bound, Complexity.logSpace, Turing.MultiTapeTM.indicator}
\difficulty{5}
Let $L$ be a language of bit strings, let $A$ be a register program with $m$ registers
and finitely many states, and let $\ell_0$ be its initial state. Suppose there are $d$
oracle languages $A_0,\ldots,A_{d-1}$, each decidable in logarithmic space, and natural
numbers $C_0,c_0$. Assume that for every input $x$, the run from $\ell_0$ with all
registers zero halts with the correct membership answer for $L$, and every configuration
before halting satisfies the program's side conditions and has every register value at
most $C_0(|x|+1)^{c_0}$. Then $L$ is decidable in logarithmic space.
\end{theorem}
